our_argument_summary: WIN-049 rebuts the dome on K1 (23.93 h) on two independent grounds. Physics: K1 is the luni-solar diurnal constituent that requires a smooth latitude-dependent declination forcing from a distant moon (d/R ≫ 1); the dome’s local moon at altitude 2,534 km (d/R≈0.13) produces a localized tidal spike rather than the smooth global diurnal-inequality distribution K1 generates. Post-hoc: dashboard registers Predicted=Observed=23.9345 h at 0.01% tolerance, both deployed as static catalogue values (raw-text/08-live-power.txt lines 216-218), so the comparison is constant-equals-constant and the value pre-dates the dome model (Doodson 1921). Verdict: Self-Contradicted, holds.

holes_found.description: Quantitative claim "1.48% at the equator" in detail_evidence lacks geometric definition and does not reproduce under the falloff law the same sentence cites. detail_evidence explicitly says "we apply the Newtonian gravitational gradient (1/r^3) as a baseline" (this is in the sibling WIN-050; the same 1.48% figure also appears in WIN-049 by the same logic). Under that falloff law and h=2,534 km, the vertical tidal-force ratio h^3/r^3 gives: 9.24% at 5,000 km offset (matches the "9%" claim — verified this cycle), but only 0.20% at the disc edge (x=20,015 km) and 0.74% at globe-equivalent antipodal distance (x≈12,742 km). 1.48% under h^3/r^3 corresponds to x ≈ 10,005 km — an offset that has no obvious natural meaning in the dome’s flat-disc geometry (it is roughly halfway from sub-lunar point to disc edge). A dome defender or numerate skeptic could ask "which equator?" and our text has no answer.
holes_found.recommendation: Either (a) define what "at the equator" means geometrically — e.g., "observer at the dome’s tropical-band equivalent circle, ~10,000 km from sub-lunar point" — OR (b) replace "1.48% at the equator" with a clearly-defined offset value (e.g., "0.2% at the disc edge (20,015 km)" which is the strongest version of the localization argument). Option (b) is preferred because it makes the spatial-concentration point even more sharply: the dome moon’s tidal force is essentially zero across most of the disc, while real K1 produces measurable inequality globally.

stronger_arguments.description: Strengthen the diurnal-inequality morphology argument: K1 is the principal contributor to the daily inequality between successive high tides at mid-to-high latitudes (e.g., Seattle, Vancouver, Anchorage), where K1+O1 dominate over M2+S2 outside the equatorial band. A near-field moon at d/R≈0.13 cannot produce the smooth latitude-dependent inequality phase observed across these stations because its tidal forcing is geometrically concentrated near the sub-lunar point. Citing 2-3 specific tide-station inequality patterns (NOAA CO-OPS harmonic constituents tables) would convert the abstract "smooth global modulation" argument into a concrete empirical attack the dome cannot answer.
sources: NOAA CO-OPS harmonic constituents tables (per-station K1/O1 amplitude and phase)
Pugh and Woodworth (2014), Sea-Level Science, Ch.4 (diurnal-inequality morphology)

kernel_of_truth.description: The dome model is correct that K1 is a real tidal constituent and that any rotating-frame-plus-moving-luminary system produces a ~24-hour periodicity (data/wins.json:049.detail_evidence — "Any model with a ~24-hour rotation and a moon that moves relative to the equator inherently produces K1"). The bare-period match is mathematically true under dome geometry as well as globe geometry. The dome’s monitor.py / dashboard can register the 23.9345 h period because that is just sidereal-day arithmetic.
kernel_of_truth.why_it_doesnt_save_claim: Clearing the bare-period bar is not the same as predicting K1. The verdict rests on two specific failures the kernel does not address. (a) Post-hoc / no-derivation: the dashboard registers Predicted=Observed=23.9345 h at 0.01% tolerance (raw-text/08-live-power.txt lines 216-218), both static catalogue values from IERS — there is no derivation from disc_radius=20,015 km / moon_altitude=2,534 km that arrives at 23.9345 h. (b) Geometric impossibility for the SHAPE of K1: K1 is defined not by its period alone but by its global diurnal-inequality distribution across latitudes, which the dome’s d/R≈0.13 geometry cannot reproduce (data/wins.json:049.detail_evidence). The kernel claim — "a moving luminary produces a diurnal periodicity" — is the easy half; predicting the global spatial distribution at observed amplitude is the hard half the dome never attempts.

advocate_mode.best_defense: The strongest dome-defender rebuttal does NOT contest the post-hoc point — that argument is airtight when both dashboard sides are catalogue lookups. Instead, the defender concedes the dashboard registration is trivial and shifts ground: "WIN-049 is over-engineered. The dome model does not need to derive 23.9345 h from disc geometry — it needs to be CONSISTENT WITH it. The K1 period is set by the sidereal day, which both dome and globe geometries agree on (the disc rotates underneath the firmament at a sidereal rate). The funwithscience.net critique is attacking a strawman: the dome model claims K1 as confirmed because the dome’s rotating-disc-plus-moving-moon geometry does, in fact, produce a 23.9345 h period — and the critique’s own kernel_of_truth concedes this. The amplitude-and-distribution argument is unfair: NO simple model derives K1’s amplitude from first principles — even globe-tidal physics gets K1’s observed amplitude from harmonic decomposition of measured tide gauge data, not from forward calculation. Holding the dome to a standard globe physics doesn’t meet is a discriminatory-power failure (Section 1.3 of the review’s own methodology)."
advocate_mode.preemptive_recommendation: Strengthen the explicit framing in detail_verdict that period-matching is NOT the claim being rebutted: "Recovering the K1 period is trivial under any rotating-frame-plus-moving-luminary geometry; the dome’s claim of confirmation rests on registering this trivial match in a dashboard with both sides set as catalogue constants. The substantive scientific test — reproducing K1’s observed amplitude (~14 cm at open ocean) and its latitude-dependent diurnal-inequality phase — is not performed by either monitor.py or the dashboard." This preempts the "unfair standard" rebuttal by explicitly naming the test that COULD be performed and showing the dome chose not to perform it.

claims_checked: Tidal force drops to 9% at 5,000 km offset
Tidal force drops to 1.48% “at the equator”
quantitative_verification.computations: Computed three claims under h^3/r^3 falloff law (the law detail_evidence and sibling WIN-050 explicitly cite). (1) d/R = 2534/20015 = 0.1266 ≈ 0.13 — VERIFIED. (2) At x=5000 km, h^3/r^3 = 2534^3 / (5000^2 + 2534^2)^1.5 = 0.0924 = 9.24% — VERIFIED ("drops to 9%"). (3) At x=20015 km (disc edge — the obvious dome-geometric reading of "the equator"), h^3/r^3 = 0.00198 = 0.20% — DOES NOT MATCH the claimed 1.48%. Solving 0.0148 = h^3/r^3 gives r/h = 4.073 → x = 2534·sqrt(4.073^2 - 1) ≈ 10,005 km, an offset with no obvious geometric meaning in dome coordinates. The "1.48% at the equator" figure is the moderate hole flagged above. (4) 23.9345 h vs IERS-published K1 = 23.9344696... h — agrees to four decimal places at displayed precision (textbook constant).
quantitative_verification.discrepancies: "1.48% at the equator" does not reproduce at the disc-edge offset (20,015 km → 0.20%) or at any obvious physical interpretation of "equator" in dome geometry. The figure corresponds to ≈10,005 km offset under the stated h^3/r^3 falloff law. Recommend rewording per the moderate hole above. All other quantitative claims (d/R, 9% at 5,000 km, 23.9345 h match) verified.
